amstar2_items.justification: Research questions (RQ1–RQ3) and Table 2 eligibility criteria define geographic location (Jakarta) and broad thematic scope (clean water challenges or solutions) rather than PICO components (population, intervention, comparator, outcome).
No prior written or registered review protocol (e.g. PROSPERO or OSF) is reported, nor are protocol deviations discussed.

Table 2 restricts publication venues to peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings (excluding purely hydrological studies without management/social links), without explaining or justifying specific empirical study designs for inclusion.

Only a single search engine (Google Scholar) was searched for 2010–2024 alongside backward reference-list snowballing; fewer than two bibliographic databases were searched and grey literature was excluded.
Single-author review; study screening and selection were performed by one individual without duplicate independent screening.
Single-author review; data extraction and thematic coding were performed by one author alone without duplicate independent extraction.
No list of excluded full-text studies with study-specific reasons for exclusion is provided.

Table 3 reports only aggregate study counts and percentages across two categorical variables (publication period and primary focus) for the claimed n=31 studies; no individual study-level characteristics table is provided, and over two-thirds of the claimed 31 studies do not even appear in the 14-item reference list.
No risk-of-bias or methodological quality appraisal tool was applied to any included study.
Sources of funding for the included primary studies were not reported.
No quantitative meta-analysis was conducted; synthesis was strictly qualitative thematic analysis.
No meta-analysis or risk-of-bias assessment was conducted.
Risk of bias and methodological quality of individual primary studies were neither assessed nor accounted for when interpreting thematic findings.
Although pre-2010 and post-2010 themes are contrasted narratively, empirical or methodological heterogeneity across individual studies is neither systematically reported nor explained.
No quantitative synthesis was conducted, so statistical publication-bias testing is not applicable (though the author briefly notes omitting NGO/government grey literature as a limitation).

In the Acknowledgements (p. 12), the author explicitly declares that no specific funding was received, the work was conducted independently, and views expressed do not reflect official Bappenas government policy.

raw_response.methodological_notes: 1. Scope & Criterion 2/3 Assessment: Substantively, S344 squarely addresses narrow Criterion 2 by examining legal, contractual, and regulatory rules governing urban water access in Jakarta—specifically the 1998–2023 Public-Private Partnership (PPP) concession contracts, the 2023 remunicipalization handover to public utility PAM JAYA, regulatory failure to enforce groundwater extraction bans, tariff governance, and informal settlement exclusion. Methodologically (Criterion 3), although self-described as a 'systematic literature review' (and 'hybrid systematic and backward-searching review') with search terms, Table 2 eligibility criteria, and a PRISMA diagram, it functions as a critically flawed qualitative/scoping-style thematic narrative rather than a rigorous systematic synthesis. 2. Severe Reporting Discrepancy on Included Studies: The paper claims n=31 included studies (27 contemporary 2010–2024 studies from Google Scholar plus 4 pre-2010 foundational studies from backward snowballing; p. 5 & Table 3), yet provides no study-by-study characteristics table or appendix, and the entire References list (p. 13) contains only 14 entries total. Of those 14 references, only 8 ([4], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [13], [14]) are cited in Section 3 Results/Discussion as synthesized studies; 3 others ([3] Fulazzaky 2014, [5] World Bank 2006, [11] Takagi et al. 2016) appear only in Section 1 Introduction or Table 1 illustrative indicators, and 3 ([1], [2], [12]) are general urban or methodological citations. Consequently, at least 20–23 of the claimed 31 included studies are completely unidentifiable and uncited. 3. Additional Editorial/Methodological Red Flags: Single-author screening and coding without protocol registration or risk-of-bias assessment; reliance solely on Google Scholar; duplicate section headings in Section 1.1/1.3, 4.1/4.2, and 4.2.1/4.2.2; and unedited prompt/placeholder prose printed beneath Figure 1 ('The diagram would show...').
